subject: physics
question_text: A man runs across the roof of a tall building and jumps horizontally on to the lower roof of an adjacent building. If his speed is 9 m s⁻¹, the horizontal distance between the buildings is 10 m and the height difference between the roofs is 9 m, will he be able to land on the next building? (take g = 10 m s⁻²)

verification.note: Unit 3 has NO Long Answer section in either source book, so no 8-mark form is invented. The Fastrack (pp.6-8) lists 4 Very Short Answer and 6 Short Answer questions plus a PROBLEMS section; the TSBIE Basic Learning Material (pp.4-5) has a Short Answer section ONLY (5 questions) and no VSAQ section. The mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. SECTION NOTE: the Fastrack files this as PROBLEM 3 in its problems section, but the TSBIE Basic Learning Material lists it as Short Answer question 5 (p.5). A book sources it as an SAQ, so it ships as one — the same promotion precedent as the Unit 8 problem the AP paper asked. The other three Fastrack problems for this unit stay deferred.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Motion in a Straight Line · 4 marks

steps.label: The fall time
lines: He leaves horizontally, so his initial vertical
velocity is zero and he falls h = 9 m.
steps.why: The horizontal speed plays no part in the fall, so the time in the air is fixed entirely by the 9 m drop.
common_mistakes: Using the 9 m s⁻¹ speed in the vertical equation. The 9 m and the 9 m s⁻¹ are different quantities that happen to share a number.

recall.must_convey: That the fall time comes from h equals half g t squared, giving t as root 1.8 seconds.

steps.memory_tip: The drop sets the clock. 9 m and 9 m s⁻¹ share a digit and nothing else.
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Keep √1.8 rather than rounding early.

steps.label: The horizontal range
lines: Horizontally he moves at a constant 9 m s⁻¹:
steps.why: There is no horizontal acceleration, so the horizontal distance is simply speed multiplied by the time already found.
common_mistakes: Applying an acceleration horizontally. Nothing pushes him forward or back once he leaves the roof.

recall.must_convey: That the horizontal range is u times t, which is 9 times root 1.8, about 12.06 metres.

steps.memory_tip: No horizontal force, so R = u × t. Nothing more.
steps.margin_note: Carry the number to two decimals before comparing.

steps.label: The verdict
lines: Required distance = 10 m, available R = 12.06 m

lines.text: R > 10 m, so yes, he lands on the roof

steps.why: The comparison is the answer to the question. A range without a comparison leaves the question unanswered.
common_mistakes: Stopping at R = 12.06 m and never comparing it with the 10 m gap.

recall.must_convey: That the range of about 12 metres exceeds the 10 metre gap, so he does land on the next building.

steps.memory_tip: Always compare with the 10 m gap. The comparison IS the answer.
steps.margin_note: Write both numbers side by side, then the verdict.

insider_note: The TSBIE material lists this as a Short Answer question, so it is worth full working. Compare the range with 10 m and give a verdict.
